svg.title: The M × N dot-product hotspot
svg.desc: On the left, a nested loop scores every query against every stored vector by calling dot(), whose inner loop does one multiply-add per double. On the right, a table has a row for each of four queries, q1 to q4, and a column for each of six stored vectors, v1 to v6. First, one dot product runs slowly: the inner loop steps eight times, and the cell for q1 and v1 fills with 0.80. Then the loop takes every other pair in turn, row by row, and each cell fills with its score while the counters climb to 24 dot products and 192 multiply-adds. Last, the inner loop is marked as the hotspot: M times N times D, or 4 times 6 times 8, gives 192 multiply-adds.
svg.text: Scoring M queries against N stored vectors takes M × N dot products, and their multiply-adds take most of the time.
the scoring loop, one dot() call per pair
static double dot(double[] a, double[] b) {
the score table, one dot product per cell
q1 to q4: M = 4 queries, one row each
v1 to v6: N = 6 stored vectors, one column each
Score M = 4 queries against N = 6 stored vectors of D = 8 doubles. All have length 1, so a dot product is their cosine.
One pair is one dot product: the k loop does D = 8 multiply-adds, and q1 · v1 comes out at 0.80.
The nested loop repeats that for every pair, one at a time and row by row, until all 4 × 6 = 24 cells hold a score.
The 24 dot products cost 24 × 8 = 192 multiply-adds, M × N × D. They take most of the time, so the k loop is the hotspot.
Sources: openjdk.org/jeps/537 (JEP 537: Vector API) and netflixtechblog.com (Optimizing recommendation systems with JDK's Vector API).
